title: Bags and Purses

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Felt suits everyday bags because it holds its shape without a stiff lining and keeps its soft surface through years of being carried. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. A purse begins as a flat layered piece worked around a shape, so the body can come out with few seams. This page will introduce the bags and purses made in the workshop, the sizes available, and what to ask about when ordering one piece or placing a wholesale enquiry from Nepal or abroad.

title: Hats and Caps

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. A felt hat is shaped from a single seamless piece, which is what makes the material so well suited to headwear. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. The damp felt is then pulled over a form and left to dry until it keeps the curve of the crown. This introduction will explain the hat and cap styles on offer, how sizes are measured, and how to enquire about colours or a batch order. Replace it with details from the people who make them.

title: Slippers and Footwear

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Thick felt makes a warm and quiet slipper, and it is one of the oldest everyday uses for the material. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Footwear needs a denser felt than most other pieces, so it is worked for longer and shaped around a last before drying. This introduction will describe the styles of slipper available, how to choose a size, what the soles are made from, and how to ask about larger quantities for a shop.

title: Coasters and Table Mats

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Coasters and table mats are the simplest pieces to make well and the easiest way to bring handmade felt into a home. Felt is naturally absorbent and protects a table from the heat of a cup. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Sheets are then cut or rolled into patterned rounds. This introduction will explain the shapes and colours on offer, whether sets can be mixed, and how cafes, hotels and gift shops can ask about wholesale felt coasters.

title: Rugs and Floor Mats

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. A felt rug is often made from hundreds of hand-rolled balls stitched together one at a time, which gives it a soft, pebbled surface underfoot. Each ball starts as a loose tuft of wool rolled between wet, soapy palms. Stitching a large rug together takes patience and a steady hand. This introduction will describe the rug shapes and diameters available, how long a piece takes to complete, and how to discuss custom colours or a project order.

title: Cushions and Home Decor

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Felt adds texture to a room without adding clutter, and it takes dye in deep, even colour. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Cushion covers, baskets and wall pieces are built up from these sheets, sometimes with shapes felted straight into the surface rather than sewn on top. This introduction will set out the home pieces available, how they are best cared for, and how interior designers or shops can enquire about colours chosen to suit a particular space.

title: Ornaments and Toys

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Small felt figures are made by needling or rolling wool into solid shapes, so they are light, soft to hold and hard to break. Details such as faces, leaves and tails are worked in by hand, which means no two turn out exactly alike. This introduction will describe the ornaments and toys available, any seasonal ranges, the age guidance that applies to the toys, and how shops can ask about buying assorted figures in quantity for retail.

processSteps.title: Preparing the wool
processSteps.text: Sample text. Wool is sorted, cleaned, dyed and teased apart so that it lies evenly.

processSteps.title: Laying and wetting
processSteps.text: Sample text. Thin layers are laid out by hand, then wetted with warm soapy water.

processSteps.title: Rolling and shaping
processSteps.text: Sample text. Pressure and movement lock the fibres together into firm felt, which is shaped while damp.

processSteps.title: Drying and finishing
processSteps.text: Sample text. Pieces are dried, then trimmed, stitched and checked by hand.
